# The D·A·M Taxonomy {#sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy dropcap="chapter-opening"}

A system that runs slowly rarely announces why. An idle accelerator can stem from a starved input pipeline (Data), an algorithm with too little arithmetic intensity (Algorithm), or a saturated memory bus (Machine). This appendix maps profiler symptoms and measurements to the axis that binds execution, before optimization begins. Readers should arrive with the three axes from the opening chapters and the iron law that quantifies them.

## How to Use This Appendix {.unnumbered}

Use the D·A·M taxonomy\index{DAM taxonomy@D·A·M taxonomy!appendix refresher} when a system misses a performance, cost, or quality target and the cause is not yet clear. Work through the framework in four passes:

1. **State the symptom and operating budget**: Record the missed end-to-end target, workload, and deployment context.
2. **Localize the candidate axis or boundary**: Use @tbl-dam-components-ref for a first pass and @tbl-dam-intersections when the evidence crosses axes.
3. **Test the hypothesis**: Map the evidence to the iron law and arithmetic intensity, then gather confirming measurements with @tbl-dam-troubleshooting and @tbl-dam-tooling.
4. **Intervene and remeasure**: Choose a lever from @tbl-bottleneck-actions, repeat the end-to-end measurement, and score the result with @tbl-dam-scorecard. If the target does not improve, revise the hypothesis.

@Tbl-dam-lookup maps each common need to the section that answers it. In every case the axis label is a hypothesis, not a verdict. The axes overlap, and a useful diagnosis may name both a dominant axis and a boundary effect.

## The Three Axes {#sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-diagnostic-summary-9f73}

When a training step stalls or a serving call misses its latency budget, the cause can sit in JPEG decoding on the host, quadratic attention work in the model, or a saturated memory bus on the accelerator. The taxonomy separates those causes along the three axes of the iron law of ML systems (@sec-introduction-iron-law-ml-systems-c32a): Data is what the model learns from and what the pipeline must deliver, Algorithm is the computation the model performs, and Machine is the hardware that executes that computation. @Tbl-dam-components-ref summarizes the role, primary physical constraint, and core optimization pathway for each axis.

```{=latex}
\begingroup
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
```

| **Axis**          |              **Role**              |    **Physical Constraint**    | **High-Leverage Optimization**                     |
|:------------------|:----------------------------------:|:-----------------------------:|:---------------------------------------------------|
| **Data (D)**      |     What the model learns from     | Volume, quality, arrival rate | Data Selection (@sec-data-selection)               |
| **Algorithm (A)** | The computation the model performs |  Operations and dependencies  | Model Compression (@sec-model-compression)         |
| **Machine (M)**   |   The hardware that executes it    |      Compute, memory, I/O     | Hardware Acceleration (@sec-hardware-acceleration) |

: **D·A·M Axis Reference**: Each axis maps to a constraint class and optimization strategy. Form a hypothesis, confirm it with measurements, then follow the chapter pointer. {#tbl-dam-components-ref tbl-colwidths="[13,23,30,34]"}

```{=latex}
\endgroup
```

This first-pass separation is useful, but production systems rarely suffer from a single axis-centered bottleneck. More often, the problem sits at the boundary between two axes, as when a data format choice determines whether the accelerator can be saturated or a pruning strategy changes the memory access pattern. Handling these cases requires mapping the intersections.

## Axis Intersections {#sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-intersection-landscape-0d6e}

The conceptual Venn overlaps in @fig-ai-triad introduce the intersections of machine learning systems; the operational version is a diagnostic triad of Data, Algorithm, and Machine joined by bidirectional coupling (@fig-dam-axis-triad). To diagnose a production bottleneck, an engineer first identifies which axis currently binds the workload, then uses the two incident edges to predict how an intervention will change memory, compute, or I/O pressure on the other two axes.


In the D·A·M acronym, Data, Algorithm, and Machine name the three diagnostic axes rather than single-letter algebraic variables; formal quantities follow the notation chapter, where $\DatasetSize$ denotes logical dataset size (samples or tokens) and $\DataVolume$ denotes physical data volume moved (bytes).

The axis-centered zones contain concepts that belong primarily to one axis: storage formats and distributions emphasize Data, loss functions and gradients emphasize Algorithm, and silicon physics and peak FLOP/s emphasize Machine. Single-domain expertise can introduce them, but deployed behavior may still depend on the other axes.

The pairwise intersections\index{DAM taxonomy@D·A·M taxonomy!axis intersections} are where systems thinking begins. At $\DataTaxonomyAxis\cap \AlgorithmTaxonomyAxis$ (*What to Learn From*), data selection, curriculum learning, active learning, and scaling laws (@sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-scaling-laws-journey-4085) couple information content to algorithmic capacity, because adding data that the model cannot absorb wastes compute while choosing architectures that outstrip available data wastes engineering time. Whereas that boundary governs statistical efficiency, $\DataTaxonomyAxis\cap \MachineTaxonomyAxis$ (*How to Move Information*) governs physical delivery through I/O bandwidth, prefetching strategies, data formats, and the energy-movement invariant, where data gravity manifests because the cost of moving bytes through the memory hierarchy decides whether the machine stays fed. Once data reaches the device, $\AlgorithmTaxonomyAxis\cap \MachineTaxonomyAxis$ (*How to Execute Efficiently*) links mathematical structure to hardware execution across quantization, pruning, kernel fusion, mixed precision, and computational graph optimization, explaining why a pruning scheme that cuts FLOPs while fragmenting memory access can still run slower on silicon.

The center, $\DataTaxonomyAxis\cap \AlgorithmTaxonomyAxis\cap \MachineTaxonomyAxis$, is where all three axes converge. The iron law, the roofline model, end-to-end training loops, serving pipelines, and holistic benchmarking all require simultaneous reasoning about data flow, algorithmic complexity, and hardware utilization.
The intersections classify where a technique operates. Isolating which axis actively throttles a workload requires translating these relationships into wall-clock execution time, which is the role of the iron law.

## Iron Law Mapping {#sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-iron-law-mapping-05db}

For any workload, the iron law\index{Iron law of ML systems!appendix refresher} connects the D·A·M axes to execution time $\Time$ (seconds) in two steps. First, at the workload level (@eq-intro-dam-iron-law), time factors multiplicatively across the three axes:
$$ \Time = \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{Samples}}{\text{Task}}\right)}_{\text{Data}} \times \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Sample}}\right)}_{\text{Algorithm}} \times \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{Seconds}}{\text{FLOP}}\right)}_{\text{Machine}} $$
where the product of the Data and Algorithm factors sets the total arithmetic work $\Operations = (\text{Samples/Task}) \times (\text{FLOPs/Sample})$ in FLOPs. Second, for serialized execution phases (@eq-intro-iron-law), unpacking how the machine executes those operations maps work across the D·A·M interfaces into three physical time terms, where $\DataVolume$ is bytes moved, $\Bandwidth$ is bytes per second, $\PeakRate$ is peak throughput in FLOP/s, $\EfficiencyHw$ is dimensionless hardware efficiency, and $\Latency$ is fixed overhead in seconds:
$$ \Time= \underbrace{ \frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth} }_{\text{Data/Machine}} + \underbrace{ \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw} }_{\text{Algorithm/Machine}} + \underbrace{ \Latency }_{\text{Cross-axis overhead}} $$

Dividing this serialized decomposition by $\Operations$ (and substituting arithmetic intensity $\ArithmeticIntensity = \Operations/\DataVolume$) expresses the realized Machine factor ($\text{Seconds/FLOP}$) directly in terms of the three physical bottlenecks:
$$ \frac{\text{Seconds}}{\text{FLOP}} = \frac{\Time}{\Operations} = \underbrace{\frac{1}{\ArithmeticIntensity \cdot \Bandwidth}}_{\text{Memory time per FLOP}} + \underbrace{\frac{1}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw}}_{\text{Compute time per FLOP}} + \underbrace{\frac{\Latency}{\Operations}}_{\text{Overhead per FLOP}} $$

Algorithm and Machine share the compute term, separated by which variable the engineer controls. Reducing the total operations ($\Operations$) is a Data or Algorithm lever, while reducing the realized time per operation ($\text{Seconds/FLOP}$) by raising peak throughput ($\PeakRate$), utilization ($\EfficiencyHw$), or bandwidth ($\Bandwidth$) is a Machine lever.

The dominant measured cost appears in one of these terms. A slow system may move too much data ($\DataVolume$), lack bandwidth ($\Bandwidth$), execute too many operations ($\Operations$), fail to use the hardware's peak capability ($\EfficiencyHw$), or pay cross-axis overhead ($\Latency$). A workload whose time is dominated by $\Latency$ is overhead-bound: kernel launches, dispatch, and synchronization, not bytes or arithmetic, set its pace. The levers below map specific optimizations to the variables they improve.

### Component levers {#sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-component-levers-d441}

*   **Data lever**: Reducing the samples processed per task ($\text{Samples/Task}$, which shrinks $\Operations$) or the moved bytes ($\DataVolume$) through deduplication and selection, or increasing I/O bandwidth ($\Bandwidth$).
*   **Algorithm lever**: Reducing operations per sample ($\text{FLOPs/Sample}$, and thus $\Operations$) through pruning, distillation, or architectural refinement, or reducing the bytes each weight and activation occupies through lower-precision representation. Quantization is an Algorithm choice that shrinks the Data/Machine term $\DataVolume$ and may raise hardware throughput $\PeakRate$, lowering $\text{Seconds/FLOP}$ without reducing operation count.
*   **Machine lever**: Lowering $\text{Seconds/FLOP}$ by increasing peak throughput ($\PeakRate$), memory bandwidth ($\Bandwidth$), or the utilization factor ($\EfficiencyHw$) via kernel fusion and scheduling.

### From sum to max {#sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-dam-coordination-sum-max-92bb}

The additive iron law represents sequential execution\index{Iron law of ML systems!sequential execution}. Let $\SequentialExecutionTime$ denote time without overlap and $\PipelinedExecutionTime$ denote measured time with overlap. Overlap can move the sum toward a max, but dependencies, contention, and incomplete overlap keep the measured time above this ideal lower bound:
$$ \SequentialExecutionTime= \frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth} + \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw} + \Latency \quad \xrightarrow{\text{overlap}} \quad \PipelinedExecutionTime\geq \max\left(\frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth}, \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw}\right) + \Latency $$

Compute should overlap with data movement wherever dependencies allow. @Tbl-dam-overlap summarizes key D·A·M coordination techniques that overlap work across axes.

| **Technique**           | **D·A·M Axes Overlapped**    | **Implementation**                                             |
|:------------------------|:-----------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Prefetching**         | D overlaps M                 | DataLoader with `prefetch_factor`, `pin_memory=True`           |
| **CUDA Streams**        | D overlaps M                 | Separate streams for H2D transfer and compute                  |
| **Async Gradient Sync** | M (communication) overlaps A | Overlap bucketed AllReduce with remaining backward computation |
| **Double Buffering**    | D overlaps M                 | Fill buffer N+1 while computing on buffer N                    |

: **D·A·M Overlap Techniques**: Each technique overlaps work across axes, moving sequentially added Data/Machine and Algorithm/Machine time toward their ideal lower bound: the larger of the two terms. Dependencies and contention limit realized overlap. {#tbl-dam-overlap tbl-colwidths="[19,27,54]"}

Overlaps provide the greatest relative speedup when the D·A·M time terms are reasonably balanced. If one term dominates (for example, a severely bandwidth-bound kernel), overlapping the smaller term with the larger yields negligible gain, because the max is still set by the same bottleneck. This balance occurs near $\DataVolume/\Bandwidth \approx \Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw)$. The overhead term is treated separately below.

::: {#psp-appendix-dam-overhead-cannot-hide .callout-perspective title="The overhead that cannot hide"}

The unhidden latency term $\Latency$ (kernel launch, synchronization barriers, Python dispatch) contains serialization points that cannot be fully overlapped. Kernel fusion can reduce this term by combining operations, but it does not eliminate all launch, scheduling, or synchronization overhead.

:::

The iron law quantifies the time each term consumes. Whether data movement or arithmetic sets the ceiling for a given kernel depends on the ratio of the two, which is arithmetic intensity.

## Arithmetic Intensity Boundary {#sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-arithmetic-intensity-boundary-7f5e}

Doubling an accelerator's peak FLOP/s leaves a kernel no faster if the arithmetic units spend most of each cycle waiting for bytes from memory. The boundary between the Data/Machine memory term and the Algorithm/Machine compute term is set by the arithmetic intensity[^fn-arithmetic-intensity-ratio] ($\ArithmeticIntensity$) of the workload. A kernel whose intensity falls below the hardware's ridge point $\PeakRate/\Bandwidth$ is **bandwidth-bound**, the regime the roofline literature calls *memory-bound*; this book keeps the bandwidth name so the regime is not confused with running out of memory capacity. A kernel above the ridge point is compute-bound.

[^fn-arithmetic-intensity-ratio]: **Arithmetic intensity**\index{Arithmetic intensity!appendix refresher}: This book uses the term for floating-point operations per byte transferred. @williams2009 calls the measured DRAM quantity *operational intensity* in the Roofline Model. Comparing the workload ratio with the hardware ridge point ($\PeakRate/\Bandwidth$) gives an upper-bound diagnosis of bandwidth- versus compute-bound execution.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: dam-ridge-decode
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ H100 RIDGE POINT VS. GPT-2 XL DECODE INTENSITY
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-arithmetic-intensity-boundary-7f5e,
# │          paragraph immediately below.
# │
# │ Goal:    Place the bandwidth-bound lighthouse on one side of the reference
# │          accelerator's ridge point.
# │ Show:    H100 dense FP16 ridge point; GPT-2 XL batch-one decode intensity;
# │          per-token weight-read time vs. arithmetic time.
# │ How:     Registry H100 peak and HBM bandwidth; registry GPT-2 XL parameters
# │          and per-token forward FLOPs at FP16 weights.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Models, Hardware, BYTES_FP16, GB
from mlsysim.core.units import flop, byte, millisecond, microsecond
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_arithmetic_intensity, fmt_memory, fmt_time

class DamRidgeDecode:
    """Reference-accelerator ridge point against GPT-2 XL batch-one decode."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    h100 = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    gpt2 = Models.Language.GPT2

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    ridge = h100.ridge_point().to(flop / byte)
    peak = h100.compute.precision_flops["fp16_dense"]
    weights = gpt2.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)
    token_flops = gpt2.inference_flops
    decode_intensity = (token_flops / weights).to(flop / byte)
    weight_read = (weights / h100.memory.bandwidth).to(millisecond)
    token_compute = (token_flops / peak).to(microsecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(290 < ridge.magnitude < 300, f"Prose says the H100 ridge is about 295 FLOP/byte, got {ridge}.")
    check(abs(decode_intensity.magnitude - 1.0) < 0.01, f"Prose says decode does about 1 FLOP per weight byte, got {decode_intensity}.")
    check(decode_intensity.magnitude * 100 < ridge.magnitude, "Prose says decode sits more than two orders of magnitude below the ridge.")
    check(0.8 < weight_read.magnitude < 1.0, f"Prose says the weight read takes about 0.9 ms, got {weight_read}.")
    check(2.5 < token_compute.magnitude < 3.5, f"Prose says the arithmetic takes about 3 us, got {token_compute}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    ridge_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(round(ridge.magnitude) * flop / byte, unit=flop / byte, precision=0)
    weights_gb_str = fmt_memory(weights, unit=GB, precision=0)
    decode_intensity_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(decode_intensity, unit=flop / byte, precision=0)
    weight_read_ms_str = fmt_time(weight_read, unit="millisecond", precision=1)
    token_compute_us_str = fmt_time(round(token_compute.magnitude) * microsecond, unit="microsecond", precision=0)
```

The reference accelerator places the boundary concretely. An H100's dense FP16 ridge point is about `{python} DamRidgeDecode.ridge_str`. GPT-2 XL decoding one token at batch one reads all `{python} DamRidgeDecode.weights_gb_str` of its FP16 weights and reaches an arithmetic intensity of only about `{python} DamRidgeDecode.decode_intensity_str`, more than two orders of magnitude below the ridge. With kernel launches captured into a replayable graph (@sec-ml-frameworks-hybrid-approaches-jit-compilation-8954), the weight read takes about `{python} DamRidgeDecode.weight_read_ms_str` while the arithmetic needs about `{python} DamRidgeDecode.token_compute_us_str`, so a faster arithmetic unit would leave the per-token time unchanged. @Sec-hardware-acceleration-roofline-model-42ff develops the ridge point, hardware balance, and the regimes on either side of it, @sec-appdx-machine-foundations-roofline-model-2529 carries the worked roofline template, and @sec-model-serving-decode-floor-7d3a turns the weight read into the decode floor a serving system plans around.

The roofline gives an upper performance bound when traffic and achieved rates are measured consistently. During a production incident, screening heuristics point to the measurements to collect first, which is where diagnosis begins.

## Diagnosing a Bottleneck {#sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-diagnosing-bottleneck-c4e1}

When a benchmark or production service misses its target, diagnosis narrows the search in four passes: fast screening heuristics first, then confirming hardware counters and profiler traces, targeted interventions on the binding term, and a stopping scorecard that decides when to stop optimizing.

### Screening rules of thumb {#sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-rules-thumb-f94f}

Under incident pressure there is rarely time to solve the full iron law. Quantitative heuristics narrow the search space quickly; the thresholds below are screening signals to check against profiler traces and hardware counters, not conclusions.

*   **Low accelerator utilization (< 80 percent)**: Screen for data, CPU, or launch starvation. Confirm with input-pipeline wait, host CPU saturation, memory-bandwidth counters, and trace gaps.
*   **High accelerator utilization (> 95 percent)**: Treat this as machine bound only if compute units are busy and memory bandwidth is not saturated. If memory bandwidth is saturated, the bottleneck is still on the Data/Machine boundary.
*   **Batch size of one**: Treat this as a warning that launch or dispatch overhead may dominate; confirm with traces before labeling the algorithm itself the bottleneck.
*   **Low arithmetic intensity (below ridge point)**: The workload is likely bandwidth-bound (Data/Machine boundary). The precise boundary is $\PeakRate/\Bandwidth$ and depends on hardware and precision.
*   **Development-production mismatch**: Treat data drift as one hypothesis alongside configuration, load, dependency, and runtime differences.

Common industry labels cross the axes. Bandwidth-bound execution sits on the Data/Machine boundary because both bytes moved and available bandwidth matter. Compute-bound execution couples Algorithm work with Machine throughput. Overhead-bound execution may reflect algorithmic serial depth, runtime dispatch, synchronization, or queueing. A screened candidate becomes a diagnosis only when a measurement confirms it.

### Confirming the hypothesis {#sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-production-troubleshooting-02fb}

@Tbl-dam-troubleshooting maps common production failure modes to candidate axes and the measurements that validate them.

| **Symptom**                     | **Hypothesis**             | **Confirm With**                                  | **Act After Confirmation**                    |
|:--------------------------------|:---------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------|
| **Low Accelerator Utilization** | Data/host starvation       | Trace gaps; loader, CPU, storage, launch counters | Prefetch, parallelize, or cut launches.       |
| **High Latency (p99)**          | Algorithm/runtime/queue    | Phase p99 and queue depth                         | Optimize the dominant phase.                  |
| **High Training Cost**          | Low useful-work efficiency | MFU, communication, idle time                     | Reduce the largest loss or resize.            |
| **High Inter-GPU Overhead**     | Communication bound        | Device trace; collective gaps                     | Bucket AllReduce; tune data-parallel overlap. |
| **Out-of-Memory (OOM)**         | Algorithm/Machine fit      | Peak weights, states, activations                 | Checkpoint, shard, quantize, or shrink batch. |

: **D·A·M Diagnostic Matrix**: First hypotheses and measurements for common failures. Confirm the binding component before intervening. {#tbl-dam-troubleshooting tbl-colwidths="[25,21,29,25]"}

Each measurement in the matrix comes from a concrete hardware or runtime counter. @Tbl-dam-tooling connects the D·A·M components to the profiling utilities that expose them; @sec-model-training-identifying-bottlenecks-f57f develops the top-down profiling method these tools serve.

| **Axis**      | **Key Metric**                        | **Primary Tool**         | **Secondary Tool**            |
|:--------------|:--------------------------------------|:-------------------------|:------------------------------|
| **Data**      | Batch Load and Wait Time              | Framework profiler trace | `iostat`, `pidstat` (I/O/CPU) |
| **Algorithm** | FLOPs, Model Depth                    | PyTorch Profiler         | DeepSpeed Flops Profiler      |
| **Machine**   | Accelerator Utilization, SM Occupancy | Nsight Compute           | `nvidia-smi`, Nsight Systems  |

: **D·A·M Tooling Map**: Profiling utilities for diagnosing bottlenecks along each D·A·M axis. Start with the primary tool for quick triage; use secondary tools for deep-dive analysis when the primary tool's output is inconclusive. {#tbl-dam-tooling tbl-colwidths="[12,37,20,31]"}

Once the measurements confirm which term binds, the remaining question is which optimization will move it.

### Acting on the binding term {#sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-bottleneck-diagnostic-3fc9}

Optimizations must target the confirmed binding term. @Tbl-bottleneck-actions covers the four regimes the book's lighthouse workloads occupy, plus the overhead-bound regime that any of them enters when the fixed latency term dominates. The compute, bandwidth, and overhead rows are named by terms of the iron law. Capacity-bound and power-bound workloads are limited by preconditions the time equation assumes are already met, that the working set fits in memory and that the energy budget can pay for the run, so either can decide feasibility before any time term is evaluated (@sec-ml-systems-workload-archetypes-fd10). For each regime, the table contrasts the interventions that yield end-to-end gains against those that waste engineering effort.

| **Regime**          |                   **Binding Term**                  | **Lighthouse**                                        | **Optimization That Works**                                                                           | **Optimization That Is Wasted**                                            |
|:--------------------|:---------------------------------------------------:|:------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Compute-bound**   |    $\Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw)$    | ResNet-50; MobileNetV2; GPT-2 XL training             | Better kernels, Tensor Cores, faster accelerator, lower precision                                     | More memory bandwidth (not the binding term)                               |
| **Bandwidth-bound** |               $\DataVolume/\Bandwidth$              | GPT-2 and Llama decode                                | Quantization; structured pruning; batching for weight reuse; fusion that removes intermediate traffic | Faster accelerator (more FLOP/s will not help)                             |
| **Overhead-bound**  |                      $\Latency$                     | Any workload served at batch one; small eager kernels | Batch within the latency budget; capture graphs; fuse or dispatch asynchronously; reduce serial depth | More compute or bandwidth unless the trace shows it binding                |
| **Capacity-bound**  | $\TotalMemoryFootprint$ vs. $\DeviceMemoryCapacity$ | DLRM embedding tables                                 | Shard or offload tables; quantize; checkpoint activations; shrink the batch                           | More FLOP/s or bandwidth before the working set fits                       |
| **Power-bound**     |       $\TotalEnergy$ per inference vs. budget       | Keyword spotting                                      | Integer arithmetic; fewer bytes moved per inference; duty cycling; smaller models                     | Higher peak FLOP/s that raises power without lowering energy per inference |

: **What Works vs. What Is Wasted**: Optimizing a nonbinding term yields little or no end-to-end improvement. A bandwidth-bound language model will not benefit from additional peak FLOP/s alone, though an accelerator with more memory bandwidth may help. Capacity and power limits act before time does, so they are checked first. {#tbl-bottleneck-actions tbl-colwidths="[13,17,16,29,25]"}

The lighthouse column names each regime's home workload, and a workload can cross regimes. GPT-2's decode is bandwidth-bound, yet its training is compute-bound (@sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-case-3-compute-wall-machine-3a0a), and ResNet-50, compute-bound in its kernels, becomes input-bound when the data pipeline cannot keep pace (@sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-case-1-starving-accelerator-data-9a56). @Sec-ml-frameworks-dispatch-tax develops the dispatch overhead behind the overhead-bound row, and @sec-hardware-acceleration-power-thermal-management-6c00 develops the power envelope behind the last. A repaired system still needs a verdict on whether it is good enough, which is what the scorecard supplies.

### Scoring the system {#sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-dam-scorecard-94e9}

Raw profiler metrics (utilization percentages, FLOP counts, bandwidth measurements) mean little until compared with the workload's targets. The efficiency indicators of the D·A·M scorecard\index{DAM taxonomy@D·A·M taxonomy!scorecard} in @tbl-dam-scorecard set those targets and show whether a repaired system can stop or must keep investigating. They are screening signals, not universal grades. Model FLOPs utilization (MFU)[^fn-mfu-hardware-scorecard] is especially useful for large-model training.

[^fn-mfu-hardware-scorecard]: **MFU**\index{Model FLOPs utilization!appendix refresher}: The ratio of achieved model FLOP/s to the hardware's theoretical peak FLOP/s, introduced in the PaLM paper [@chowdhery2022palm]. Unlike raw accelerator utilization (which counts any work the accelerator performs), MFU measures model computation rate relative to peak hardware throughput, so non-model work and system overhead are not counted as achieved model FLOPs. @Sec-model-training-identifying-bottlenecks-f57f develops MFU as a training diagnostic.

```{=latex}
\begingroup
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{2.7}
```

| **Axis**      | **Metric**     |                       **Definition**                       |    **Investigate**     |   **Strong Signal**   |
|:--------------|:---------------|:----------------------------------------------------------:|:----------------------:|:---------------------:|
| **Data**      | I/O Overhead   |  $\dfrac{\text{Data Wait Time}}{\text{Total Step Time}}$   |    $>$ 10% (screen)    |    $<$ 1% (strong)    |
| **Algorithm** | Avoidable Work |      Profiler or ablation finds redundant operations       |  Redundant work found  | End-to-end work falls |
| **Machine**   | MFU            | $\dfrac{\text{Achieved model FLOP/s}}{\text{Peak FLOP/s}}$ | $<$ 30% (large models) | $>$ 50% (same regime) |

: **D·A·M Screening Indicators**: Context-dependent signals for investigation, not universal grades. {#tbl-dam-scorecard tbl-colwidths="[14,16,36,17,17]"}

```{=latex}
\endgroup
```

The four steps work only when they are followed in order. In practice, teams under deadline pressure skip the confirming step and optimize the wrong axis with confidence, and these failure modes are common enough to deserve their own names.

## Anti-Patterns {#sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-antipatterns-72e1}

Before committing to complex kernel optimizations, watch for these common traps that waste engineering cycles.

*   **The hardware crutch**: Buying faster accelerators (*Machine*) to fix a slow Python data loader (*Data*). The new hardware will just idle faster.
*   **The model twiddle**: Changing neural architectures (*Algorithm*) when the bottleneck is actually network bandwidth or disk I/O.
*   **The premature optimizer**: Writing custom CUDA kernels (*Machine*) before verifying if the Algorithm is simply doing too many unnecessary operations.

Each anti-pattern follows the same root cause: acting before diagnosing. The case studies that follow show proper diagnosis on the reference accelerator, starting from a confusing symptom and narrowing to the binding term, and the first of them puts a number on the hardware crutch.

## Case Studies on H100 {#sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-dam-case-studies-593f}

The three cases below run the four-step workflow on an H100, the book's reference accelerator, each with a lighthouse workload in a regime the chapters develop: ResNet-50 starved by its input pipeline, DLRM paying launch overhead at batch one, and GPT-2 XL training against the compute term.

### Case 1: The starving accelerator (Data) {#sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-case-1-starving-accelerator-data-9a56}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: dam-case-starving-accelerator
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CASE 1: RESNET-50 INPUT PIPELINE STARVES THE ACCELERATOR
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-case-1-starving-accelerator-data-9a56.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that a host-bound input pipeline caps training throughput, so
# │          a faster accelerator lowers utilization instead of raising speed.
# │ Show:    Accelerator demand (A100, H100), pipeline supply, utilization on
# │          each, and the worker count that would balance the H100.
# │ How:     MLPerf per-accelerator ResNet-50 training throughput anchors;
# │          scenario decode rate per loader worker and worker count.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import Hardware, Literature, Models
from mlsysim.core.units import flop, second
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_count, fmt_percent, fmt_rate

class DamStarvingAccelerator:
    """ResNet-50 training demand vs. host decode supply on A100 and H100 (same model as the training chapter)."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    resnet = Models.Vision.ResNet50
    h100 = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    a100 = Hardware.Cloud.A100
    a100_demand = float(
        Literature.Benchmarks.ResNet50A100TrainThroughput
    )  # registry anchor shared with the training chapter: A100 ResNet-50 training images/s
    per_worker = 375  # scenario assumption shared with the training chapter: JPEG decode + augment per worker, images/s
    workers = math.ceil(a100_demand / per_worker)  # loader workers sized to keep the A100 fed

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    train_flops = (resnet.inference_flops * 3).to(flop).magnitude
    a100_ceiling = a100.compute.peak_flops.to(flop / second).magnitude / train_flops
    h100_ceiling = h100.compute.peak_flops.to(flop / second).magnitude / train_flops
    h100_demand = h100_ceiling * (a100_demand / a100_ceiling)
    supply = per_worker * workers
    h100_util = min(1.0, supply / h100_demand)
    a100_util = min(1.0, supply / a100_demand)
    workers_needed = math.ceil(h100_demand / per_worker)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(supply >= a100_demand, f"Prose says the configured pipeline keeps the A100 fully busy, got {supply} vs {a100_demand}.")
    check(9_800 < h100_demand < 10_400, f"Prose says the H100 needs about 10,100 images/s, got {h100_demand:.0f}.")
    check(a100_util == 1.0, "The configured pipeline must fully feed the A100.")
    check(0.30 < h100_util < 0.36, f"Prose says the H100 is busy about a third of the time, got {h100_util:.3f}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    h100_demand_str = fmt_rate(round(h100_demand, -2), "images/s", precision=0, commas=True)
    a100_demand_str = fmt_rate(a100_demand, "images/s", precision=0, commas=True)
    supply_str = fmt_rate(supply, "images/s", precision=0, commas=True)
    per_worker_str = fmt_rate(per_worker, "images/s", precision=0, commas=True)
    workers_str = fmt_count(workers, precision=0)
    workers_needed_str = fmt_count(workers_needed, precision=0)
    h100_util_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(h100_util * 100) / 100, precision=0, style="prose")
```

A team moves ResNet-50 training from an A100 to an H100 and sees no change in epoch time. A well-tuned A100 sustains about `{python} DamStarvingAccelerator.a100_demand_str`, and at the same fraction of its higher peak the H100 would train about `{python} DamStarvingAccelerator.h100_demand_str`, yet `nvidia-smi` on the new machine shows utilization oscillating far below that. Screening flags low utilization, and the trace confirms the hypothesis, showing the accelerator idle in gaps while every loader process is saturated decoding JPEGs. With `{python} DamStarvingAccelerator.workers_str` workers each decoding and augmenting about `{python} DamStarvingAccelerator.per_worker_str`, the pipeline delivers `{python} DamStarvingAccelerator.supply_str` regardless of the accelerator, a rate that kept the A100 fully busy while leaving the H100 busy only about `{python} DamStarvingAccelerator.h100_util_pct_str` of the time. Because the upgrade was the hardware crutch, the useful intervention lies upstream of the model: balancing the H100 requires about `{python} DamStarvingAccelerator.workers_needed_str` workers' worth of decode throughput, supplied by adding loader parallelism where host cores allow and by moving decode onto the accelerator, as the supply-and-demand pipeline model in @sec-model-training-data-pipeline-8e71 develops.

### Case 2: The latency cliff (cross-axis) {#sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-case-2-latency-cliff-algorithm-8ee2}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: dam-case-latency-cliff
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CASE 2: DLRM AT BATCH ONE IS OVERHEAD-BOUND
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-case-2-latency-cliff-algorithm-8ee2.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that a batch-one DLRM scoring call spends almost all its time
# │          in per-kernel overhead, so scoring candidates one at a time misses
# │          the budget while batching them meets it.
# │ Show:    Per-call overhead, embedding-read and MLP times on the H100,
# │          serial vs. batched latency for one request's candidates.
# │ How:     Registry runtime overheads and H100 bandwidth and peak; scenario
# │          kernel count, lookup count, embedding width, MLP size, candidates.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Hardware, Ops, BYTES_FP32, KB
from mlsysim.core.units import flop, millisecond, microsecond, nanosecond
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_count, fmt_memory, fmt_time

class DamLatencyCliff:
    """Overhead vs. bytes vs. FLOPs for one batch-one DLRM call on the H100."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    h100 = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    per_kernel = Ops.RuntimeOverheads.PythonDispatch + Ops.RuntimeOverheads.KernelLaunch
    kernels = 40  # scenario assumption: embedding, interaction, and MLP kernels per call
    lookups = 100  # scenario assumption: embedding vectors fetched per scored item
    emb_dim = 128  # scenario assumption: embedding width
    mlp_layers = 4  # scenario assumption: MLP depth
    mlp_width = 512  # scenario assumption: MLP width
    candidates = 200  # scenario assumption: items ranked per request
    budget = 10 * millisecond  # scenario assumption: p99 latency budget

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    peak = h100.compute.precision_flops["fp16_dense"]
    call_overhead = (kernels * per_kernel).to(millisecond)
    emb_bytes = (lookups * emb_dim * BYTES_FP32).to(KB)
    data_time = (emb_bytes / h100.memory.bandwidth).to(nanosecond)
    mlp_flops = 2 * mlp_layers * mlp_width * mlp_width * flop
    compute_time = (mlp_flops / peak).to(nanosecond)
    overhead_ratio = (call_overhead / (data_time + compute_time)).to("").magnitude
    serial = (candidates * (call_overhead + data_time + compute_time)).to(millisecond)
    batched = (call_overhead + candidates * (data_time + compute_time)).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(call_overhead.magnitude - 0.6) < 1e-9, f"Prose says each call pays 0.6 ms of overhead, got {call_overhead}.")
    check(overhead_ratio > 1e4, f"Prose says overhead exceeds bytes plus FLOPs by four orders of magnitude, got {overhead_ratio:.0f}.")
    check(119 < serial.magnitude < 121, f"Prose says serial scoring takes about 120 ms, got {serial}.")
    check(serial > budget > batched, "Prose says serial scoring misses the budget and batched scoring meets it.")
    check(0.55 < batched.magnitude < 0.65, f"Prose says batched scoring takes about 0.6 ms, got {batched}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    per_kernel_us_str = fmt_time(per_kernel, unit="microsecond", precision=0)
    kernels_str = fmt_count(kernels, precision=0)
    call_overhead_ms_str = fmt_time(call_overhead, unit="millisecond", precision=1)
    emb_kb_str = fmt_memory(emb_bytes, unit=KB, precision=1)
    data_time_ns_str = fmt_time(data_time, unit="nanosecond", precision=1)
    compute_time_ns_str = fmt_time(compute_time, unit="nanosecond", precision=1)
    candidates_str = fmt_count(candidates, precision=0)
    serial_ms_str = fmt_time(round(serial.magnitude) * millisecond, unit="millisecond", precision=0)
    batched_ms_str = fmt_time(batched, unit="millisecond", precision=1)
    budget_ms_str = fmt_time(budget, unit="millisecond", precision=0)
```

A recommendation service on an H100 must rank `{python} DamLatencyCliff.candidates_str` candidate items per request within a `{python} DamLatencyCliff.budget_ms_str` p99 budget, and it misses badly while accelerator utilization stays low because the serving code scores each candidate with its own DLRM call at batch one. Screening flags the batch size, and a trace confirms an overhead-bound regime: each call issues about `{python} DamLatencyCliff.kernels_str` kernels at about `{python} DamLatencyCliff.per_kernel_us_str` of dispatch and launch apiece, costing `{python} DamLatencyCliff.call_overhead_ms_str` before any device work happens, whereas reading `{python} DamLatencyCliff.emb_kb_str` of embeddings takes only about `{python} DamLatencyCliff.data_time_ns_str` at high-bandwidth memory (HBM) bandwidth and the multilayer perceptron (MLP) needs only about `{python} DamLatencyCliff.compute_time_ns_str` of arithmetic. Because the $\Latency$ term exceeds the other two by more than four orders of magnitude, scoring candidates one at a time multiplies that fixed tax to about `{python} DamLatencyCliff.serial_ms_str`, and a faster accelerator or wider memory bus would shrink only the nanosecond terms. Instead, batching all candidates into one call pays the overhead once to bring the request to about `{python} DamLatencyCliff.batched_ms_str`, while capturing the call as a graph shortens what remains. The cliff runs the other way too: with large tables the same model becomes capacity-bound, the embedding reads grow, and the measurements must be repeated. @Sec-model-serving-batching-helps-f1dc develops why batching amortizes this fixed cost and where the latency budget stops it.

### Case 3: The compute wall (Machine) {#sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-case-3-compute-wall-machine-3a0a}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: dam-case-compute-wall
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CASE 3: GPT-2 XL TRAINING AGAINST THE COMPUTE TERM
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-case-3-compute-wall-machine-3a0a.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that a well-fed, compute-bound training run shortens only by
# │          changing the compute term: precision (peak rate) or device count.
# │ Show:    GPT-2 XL training compute; run time on one H100 in TF32, in FP16/
# │          BF16, and on eight H100s; the BF16-to-TF32 peak ratio.
# │ How:     Registry GPT-2 XL training FLOPs, H100 per-precision peaks, and
# │          the upper MFU anchor for well-tuned large-model training.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Models, Hardware, Literature
from mlsysim.core.units import day
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_count, fmt_flops, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, fmt_time

class DamComputeWall:
    """GPT-2 XL training time on H100 under precision and device-count levers."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    gpt2 = Models.Language.GPT2
    h100 = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    mfu = Literature.Training.MfuHigh.value
    devices = 8  # scenario assumption: one eight-accelerator node

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    train_ops = gpt2.training_ops
    tf32_peak = h100.compute.precision_flops["tf32"]
    bf16_peak = h100.compute.precision_flops["fp16_dense"]
    tf32_days = (train_ops / (tf32_peak * mfu)).to(day)
    bf16_days = (train_ops / (bf16_peak * mfu)).to(day)
    node_days = (train_ops / (bf16_peak * mfu * devices)).to(day)
    precision_ratio = (bf16_peak / tf32_peak).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(69.5 < tf32_days.magnitude < 70.5, f"Prose says about 70 days in TF32, got {tf32_days}.")
    check(34.5 < bf16_days.magnitude < 35.5, f"Prose says about 35 days in BF16, got {bf16_days}.")
    check(4.0 < node_days.magnitude < 4.6, f"Prose says about 4 days on one node, got {node_days}.")
    check(round(precision_ratio) == 2, f"Prose says BF16 peak is about 2x TF32, got {precision_ratio:.2f}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    train_ops_str = fmt_flops(train_ops, precision=1)
    mfu_pct_str = fmt_percent(mfu, precision=0, style="prose")
    tf32_days_str = fmt_time(round(tf32_days.magnitude) * day, unit="day", precision=0, style="word")
    bf16_days_str = fmt_time(round(bf16_days.magnitude) * day, unit="day", precision=0, style="word")
    node_days_str = fmt_time(round(node_days.magnitude) * day, unit="day", precision=0, style="word")
    devices_str = fmt_count(devices, precision=0)
    precision_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(precision_ratio), precision=0)
```

A team trains GPT-2 XL on one H100 in TF32. Accelerator utilization is pinned near its maximum, memory-bandwidth counters are unsaturated, and the profiler reports MFU near `{python} DamComputeWall.mfu_pct_str`, the strong-signal end of the scorecard. Because the data path keeps the accelerator fed and the trace shows no dispatch gaps, the compute term binds: whereas GPT-2's home regime in serving is bandwidth-bound decode, training at batch reuses every weight across many tokens and crosses the ridge. The run needs about `{python} DamComputeWall.train_ops_str` of arithmetic, which at this efficiency takes about `{python} DamComputeWall.tf32_days_str`, so only levers on the compute term help while adding loader workers or memory bandwidth changes nothing. Lowering precision from TF32 to BF16 where numerically safe raises the H100's Tensor Core peak by about `{python} DamComputeWall.precision_mult_str` [@choquette2023], cutting the run to about `{python} DamComputeWall.bf16_days_str`, and data parallelism across the `{python} DamComputeWall.devices_str` accelerators of one node brings it to about `{python} DamComputeWall.node_days_str` before communication losses. @Sec-model-training-running-example-training-gpt2-19cd develops this workload as the training running example, including the memory limits that decide what batch fits.

Taken together, the three cases show why the same utilization number can imply different next steps. Low utilization meant a starved pipeline in the first case and dispatch overhead in the second, while high utilization in the third meant the run was already doing useful work and only the compute term could shrink. The same discipline applies when the question is not how fast the system runs but how much better the model can get.

## Scaling Laws and the Roofline {#sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-scaling-laws-vs-roofline-b290}

When a training run's held-out loss flattens despite more GPUs and longer runs, the stall can reflect either a predictable power-law return or a data-quality floor that added compute cannot move. Empirical scaling laws characterize how loss decreases as compute, data, or parameters expand, while roofline bounds identify the physical ceilings imposed by memory bandwidth and arithmetic throughput.

### Scaling laws {#sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-scaling-laws-journey-4085}

Scaling laws[^fn-scaling-law-exponent] are empirical power laws that predict how held-out loss changes as resources increase within the fitted regime. Two landmark results are Kaplan scaling [@kaplan2020scaling], which studied loss against parameter count ($\Parameters$), data ($\DatasetSize$), and total operations ($\Operations$), and Chinchilla scaling [@hoffmann2022chinchilla], which estimated a compute-optimal balance for the dense autoregressive language-model regime studied, often summarized as roughly 20 training tokens per parameter ($\DatasetSize\approx 20\Parameters$). @Sec-appdx-algorithm-chinchilla-derivation derives that balance from a parametric loss surface, so a reader can see where the tokens-per-parameter ratio comes from and which fitted exponents it depends on.

[^fn-scaling-law-exponent]: **Scaling laws**\index{Scaling laws!appendix refresher}: Empirical relationships, typically power laws with a fitted negative exponent, that predict model loss as a function of dataset size, parameter count, or compute budget. @kaplan2020scaling studied these relationships for neural language models at OpenAI; @hoffmann2022chinchilla later estimated the compute-optimal training trade-off for its studied dense language-model regime. @Sec-data-selection-computeoptimal-frontier-24ba develops the compute-optimal frontier and its data-starvation diagnostic in detail.

As planning tools, these fits estimate how held-out loss changes with compute inside the observed regime. They do not guarantee a task error-rate reduction or extrapolate unchanged across architectures and data distributions.

### The information roofline {#sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-information-roofline-destination-6426}

When held-out loss flattens below the fitted scaling trend while tokens, parameters, and compute keep growing, adding accelerators or parameters buys no further accuracy. The **information roofline**\index{Information roofline!definition} names this limit that data quality places on what a model can learn, the counterpart to the ceiling the roofline model places on how fast it computes. Because it is a diagnostic label rather than a quantitative law, that flattening pattern tells the team to examine the data before buying more hardware, using four checks to separate the causes: deduplicating the training set and remeasuring tests whether repeated examples inflated the apparent data volume, auditing a sample of labels estimates label noise, comparing per-slice validation loss exposes coverage gaps, and comparing the training and validation distributions detects shift. If loss resumes falling after cleaning or reweighting the data at fixed compute, data quality was binding; if it does not, the cause lies in optimization, model capacity, or evaluation noise, and the scaling-law fit itself should be rechecked.

For classification under a fixed data distribution and loss, the Bayes error rate[^fn-bayes-error-rate] is an irreducible error floor, not a ceiling. Noise, label ambiguity, coverage gaps, and distribution shift can create data-quality limits above that floor, but they do not define one universal slope or breakpoint.

[^fn-bayes-error-rate]: **Bayes error rate**\index{Bayes error rate!appendix refresher}: The lowest achievable error rate under 0–1 loss for any classifier on a given data distribution, determined by class priors and the overlap between class-conditional distributions [@goodfellow2016deep]. No amount of data, parameters, or compute can reduce error below this theoretical floor.

Adding accelerators or parameters is futile only after measurements establish that data quality is binding. Whether debugging a training step, evaluating hardware utilization, or planning a scaling campaign, measure which axis is binding before choosing a lever.

::: {#chk-appendix-dam-diagnosis-check .callout-checkpoint title="D·A·M diagnosis check"}

1. A training job shows 95 percent accelerator utilization but loss has plateaued for two epochs. Which D·A·M axes could be responsible, and why is utilization alone insufficient to distinguish them?
2. Your colleague suggests adding more data loader workers to a job where `nvidia-smi` shows 98 percent GPU utilization. What trace evidence is needed before deciding whether this will help?
3. An inference server meets its latency SLO at batch size 1 but fails at batch size 16. Which iron-law terms and queueing effects may have changed, and which measurements identify the binding regime?

:::

## Summary {#sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-summary-1521}

D·A·M localizes candidate causes across Data, Algorithm, and Machine. The iron law and arithmetic intensity translate those causes into time, operations, and bytes, and the four-step workflow screens, confirms, acts on, and scores them across the four lighthouse regimes, compute-bound, bandwidth-bound, capacity-bound, and power-bound, and the overhead-bound regime that a deployment choice such as batch-one serving can create. The anti-patterns and the H100 case studies show what skipping or following that workflow costs. Scaling laws and the information roofline then separate observed improvement trajectories from data-quality limits. Use the framework as a loop rather than as a label.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Where to look first"}

* Begin with cross-axis hypotheses; a symptom rarely identifies its cause.
* Translate each hypothesis into the relevant iron-law term, or the capacity or power precondition, and a measurement that could falsify it.
* Use arithmetic intensity and the scorecard to identify the binding constraint, not to assign universal grades.
* Apply the corresponding lever and remeasure end to end; a local gain that leaves the binding term unchanged is not a system improvement.

:::
